#### Re-referencing the excluded cells

Every SOH above is measured against the median of the cell's first five valid discharges. A gentler re-reference was checked on the excluded cells: the median of discharges {{rsc_mid_lo:d}}-{{rsc_mid_hi:d}}, and the beginning-of-life peak (the maximum of the first five). The SOH ceiling and the capacity-rise test are held fixed, so a cell is returned only when the reference, not the rule, was what excluded it.

| B0056 | G9 | {{rsc_b0056_first5:.1f}} | {{rsc_b0056_mid38:.1f}} | {{rsc_b0056_peak:.1f}} | no |

The gentler rule the check started from returns nothing: none of B0054, B0055 or B0056 comes back. Their capacity genuinely rises from the recorded first discharge, so the drift is in the data, not only in the reference; B0054 also stays above the ceiling. The four G7 cells return under the beginning-of-life peak alone, because their reading above the {{rsc_ceiling:.0f}}% ceiling was a high first cycle sitting above the early median rather than a real rise. No G4 cell returns under any rule: its capacity rises across the record by far more than a reference choice can explain.

The peak reference is reported and not adopted: applying it uniformly would rescale every kept cell's SOH, and a per-cell fallback would make the reference depend on the outcome it is tested against. The production reference is unchanged, so no kept cell's SOH and no reported number moves.

#### Cross-condition transfer (leave-one-group-out, partial window only)

**On the partial-discharge task the model does not transfer across conditions when it is trained on raw window features.** A BMS that only watches the partial-discharge window never sees the full discharge, so this is the honest version of the SOH question: predict SOH from the window alone.
With the full feature set, leave-one-cell-out within G1 the same ElasticNet model reaches {{cc_in_cell_en_mae:.2f}}% MAE; held out across conditions on raw window features it climbs to as much as {{cc_worst_raw_en_mae:.2f}}%. The table below is that failure, measured, not a model claim.

| Held-out group | Cells | Cycles | ElasticNet MAE (%) | XGBoost MAE (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| G1 | {{logo_g1_cells:d}} | {{logo_g1_cycles:d}} | {{logo_g1_en_mae:.2f}} | {{logo_g1_xgb_mae:.2f}} |
| G3 | {{logo_g3_cells:d}} | {{logo_g3_cycles:d}} | {{logo_g3_en_mae:.2f}} | {{logo_g3_xgb_mae:.2f}} |
| B0053 (G9) | {{logo_g9_cells:d}} | {{logo_g9_cycles:d}} | {{logo_g9_en_mae:.2f}} | {{logo_g9_xgb_mae:.2f}} |

**Cell-relative window features recover the transfer, and the model then beats the window formula on the held-out condition.** Because the groups differ in ambient temperature (G1 {{cc_g1_temp:d}} °C, G3 {{cc_g3_temp:d}} °C, G9 {{cc_g9_temp:d}} °C) and current (G1 {{cc_g1_amp:d}} A, G3 {{cc_g3_amp:d}} A, G9 {{cc_g9_amp:d}} A), the raw levels do not line up. Dividing each window quantity by the cell's own first-five-discharge median and by its current puts every cell on the same scale and makes the ElasticNet transfer to a condition it has never seen. The window formula — the window's amp-hours over that same per-cell median — is the best a BMS can do from the window alone, so it is scored on exactly the held-out cells for comparison.

| Held-out group | Cells | Cycles | window formula MAE (%) | raw ElasticNet MAE (%) | cell-relative ElasticNet MAE (%) | cell-relative XGBoost MAE (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| G1 | {{cc_g1_cells:d}} | {{cc_g1_cycles:d}} | {{cc_g1_coulomb_mae:.2f}} | {{cc_g1_raw_en_mae:.2f}} | {{cc_g1_rel_en_mae:.2f}} | {{cc_g1_rel_xgb_mae:.2f}} |
| G3 | {{cc_g3_cells:d}} | {{cc_g3_cycles:d}} | {{cc_g3_coulomb_mae:.2f}} | {{cc_g3_raw_en_mae:.2f}} | {{cc_g3_rel_en_mae:.2f}} | {{cc_g3_rel_xgb_mae:.2f}} |
| B0053 (G9) | {{cc_g9_cells:d}} | {{cc_g9_cycles:d}} | {{cc_g9_coulomb_mae:.2f}} | {{cc_g9_raw_en_mae:.2f}} | {{cc_g9_rel_en_mae:.2f}} | {{cc_g9_rel_xgb_mae:.2f}} |

B0053 is the only G9 cell the audit keeps, so its row is that cell alone, never averaged into a group. Reading it: the cell-relative ElasticNet error on B0053 is {{cc_g9_rel_en_mae:.2f}}% against the window formula's {{cc_g9_coulomb_mae:.2f}}%, and the cell-relative XGBoost error is {{cc_g9_rel_xgb_mae:.2f}}% — both beat the formula on a condition the model has never seen. On the two multi-cell groups the model also beats it cell-by-cell (G1 ElasticNet {{cc_g1_rel_en_mae:.2f}}% versus {{cc_g1_coulomb_mae:.2f}}%, G3 ElasticNet {{cc_g3_rel_en_mae:.2f}}% versus {{cc_g3_coulomb_mae:.2f}}%), though XGBoost is weaker on G1. The cell-by-cell partial-discharge section below reports the same task with leave-one-cell-out validation.

Inside a group the picture is mixed: the plain window formula is sensitive to the baseline length, while the learned models stay flat because the held-out cell is trained on siblings at the same condition. The cross-condition transfer to B0053 is where the baseline length matters for the model too: one or two opening discharges set the scale too coarsely and the error spikes, and from three discharges it settles near its floor. The practical reading: give a new cell a few discharges before trusting its cell-relative SOH.


#### Offline SOH benchmark (full feature set)

This benchmark is deliberately offline: it uses every production feature, including full-discharge signals such as duration and resistance that a BMS only observes once the discharge has finished. It is a model-to-model reference; the online task, and the only place a model is compared against a physics formula, is the partial-discharge section above. The full-discharge Coulomb row is the formula that would be used when a complete discharge is available.

#### Both methods, side by side on every held-out cell

The matcher was also scored against a fade-rate extrapolation: a straight line through the first {{rc_window:d}} measured SOH values of the cell, extended to the retirement threshold. Both are leave-one-cell-out and use the same held-out discharges, so the columns are comparable. The last numeric column is the mean absolute gap between the two methods over those discharges.

| Held-out cell | Trajectory MAE | Early-fade extrapolation MAE | Method disagreement | Fleet-lifetime baseline MAE |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| B0005 | {{rul_b0005_traj_mae:.1f}} | {{rc_b0005_extrap_mae:.1f}} | {{rc_b0005_gap:.1f}} | {{rul_b0005_base_mae:.1f}} |
| B0006 | {{rul_b0006_traj_mae:.1f}} | {{rc_b0006_extrap_mae:.1f}} | {{rc_b0006_gap:.1f}} | {{rul_b0006_base_mae:.1f}} |

No method is chosen per cell, and no cell is scored with the method that happens to win it: that would be reading the answer off the test set. Instead both methods are shown on every held-out cell and their disagreement is reported as the uncertainty. It is large — {{rc_mean_gap:.1f}} discharges on the mean, and {{rc_worst_gap:.1f}} on B0007 — because a line that overshoots a late knee and a matcher that follows reference curves can disagree by an entire lifetime. That width, not a point estimate, is the honest statement about RUL on four cells, and it is why the whole task is labelled indicative.

#### Calibrating a real 10th-to-90th band

The reference-spread band above is a quantile of the reference cells' remaining life, not a calibrated error band. The honest version calibrates the band on the other cells and measures it on a cell it never saw: for each held-out cell the offsets are the 10th and 90th percentile of the (truth - estimate) residuals pooled from the other three cells.

A 10th-to-90th band should cover four discharges in five, and this one misses by a wide margin and swings from 0.0% to 100.0% across cells. It is not fixable here: only three cells calibrate any held-out band, and one cell's residuals are correlated across its discharges, so the effective calibration sample is closer to three than to the number of points. A trustworthy calibrated band needs more cells than the four in G1; the reference spread remains the only band this dataset supports.

#### More cells that reach 80%? Yes, in the random-load groups

RUL needs a cell that actually reaches the retirement threshold, so the groups the model leaves out were checked against the same SOH rule rather than assumed dead. The NASA random-load groups G5 (B0038-B0040) and G6 (B0041-B0044) were run through it: {{rl_total:d}} cells checked, {{rl_reaches:d}} reach {{rl_threshold:d}}%, and {{rl_usable:d}} of those also pass the same ceiling/rise keep filter (B0039, B0042, B0043, B0044). So the claim that only the four G1 cells reach 80% is false in general: four more cells do. They are still not added to the model, because their load and temperature change across the record, so their features are not comparable at a single operating condition — the reason they were left out is comparability, not ageing. B0041 reaches 80% too but is excluded, because the very-low-capacity runs the dataset's own notes flag corrupt its early reference capacity, so its SOH never has a trustworthy baseline.
